title: Work smart, not hard. Or how I “waste” my $200 subscription making my city builder
author: Kiko_Production
selftext:
I'm a solo dev making a small city builder in Godot.

What I learned recently is not very glamorous: I was wasting way more time on bad approaches than on actual hard problems.

That’s also where a good chunk of my $200/month went.

For a while I kept trying to invent everything myself. I would overcomplicate pipelines, ignore basic theory, and brute-force problems that already had simpler solutions. So the subscription felt “wasted” not because the tools were bad, but because I was using them inside a bad process.

Only in the last week or so did things really click for me, mostly while working with Claude (Opus 5.5), with ChatGPT handling the art side.

The big change was this: instead of pushing harder, I started throwing bad workflows away.

**Buildings (the first 4 seconds of the video are “before”)**

My old pipeline for **one** building had eight steps: grey block-out in code, a painted isometric “master” image, four separately generated side views, checking that windows, doors and chimneys matched across views, Tripo for the mesh, texturing from those same four views, fixing mesh/scale/pivot, and then checking it again from four sides in day and night.

Every building was basically a one-off.  
Style drifted all the time.  
And if I wanted a colour variant, I had to redo half the process.

The new pipeline is much simpler:

1. ChatGPT draws one concept sheet using my style reference.
2. Claude writes a short Blender script and builds the model headless.
3. The model has no baked textures, only material names like `brick`, `roof_shingles`, or `plaster#e8c9a0`.
4. In-engine, one shader paints everything using tileable hand-painted swatches.

Those swatches are also drawn by ChatGPT and then made seamless by script.

The best part is that Claude basically talks to ChatGPT for me. I leave a ChatGPT tab open, it attaches the style reference, writes the brief, waits for the result, grabs it, makes it tileable, and puts it into the game. My role is mostly to look at the result and say “no” or “this one”.

That changed everything.

Now the style lives in a small material library instead of being rebuilt for every single asset. Anything new is in-style by default. Variants are almost free. One house can instantly have multiple wall and roof combinations without rebuilding the whole thing.

One night I went to sleep and woke up to five shops, a water tower, a house with seven variations, thirteen street props, and a community club already standing in-game.  
  
In the second part of the video, most of the buildings are simply copies of one another. In fact, using this method, I generated about 20 unique buildings in a single night.

**Grass**

Grass was another case where I made my own life harder.

I spent days trying to invent my own solution: clumps, little 3D tufts, colouring them from the ground, all that stuff. Most of it got thrown away.

Then I finally did the obvious thing: I looked up how other people solve stylized grass well.

I found a great YouTube breakdown by Dylearn, gave it to Claude, and asked it not to copy it directly, but to adapt the idea to my game’s look. It read the transcript, stepped through the video, got it wrong twice, and then on the third pass got close enough to be useful.

That was still much faster than me trying to reinvent the whole thing from scratch.

**What I took from it**  
  
1. Put style into something reusable, not into every asset.  
  
2. Before inventing a solution, spend 20 minutes checking whether someone already solved it better.  
  
3. AI is most useful to me not when it replaces taste, but when it replaces dumb repetition and still checking for errors or a bad ui ux.  
  
4. Let the models talk to each other. My job is mostly taste and direction.



The town in the video is my stress test. The first version ran at around 8–10 fps. Now it averages 100+ on an RTX 4060.

Everything is still heavily work in progress, and yes, the textures are AI-generated from my own style sheet.

Happy to answer questions about the setup.

Hey! Thanks for sharing.

Other than in-game assets, what would you say the biggest stumbling block so far?

replies.author: Kiko_Production
replies.body: Honestly, I think the hardest part is still ahead of me. I’ll need to combine dating sim mechanics with the city builder and make them feel connected. There’s also the visual novel side, figuring out scene composition, camera angles and character placement so the story scenes actually work. That’s probably going to be my biggest challenge.

replies.author: Kiko_Production
replies.body:
Here are a couple of examples: a building concept sheet.

Honestly, Opus handles most of the prompt writing for me. I explain what I want, give it my style references, and point out what needs changing. It understands that feedback pretty well and turns it into detailed prompts for ChatGPT.

My part is mostly reviewing the results and asking for adjustments, so I can’t really take credit for any clever prompt engineering here

comments.author: Briskfall
comments.body:
With LLMs, often the journey in figuring out different approach on how to make things click is the fun. I currently am in the process of trying to make things from scratch as well, as it gives me a lot of freedom to play around with ideas. Though I understand that when arriving at a road block, looking for "solved solutions" is on key to breaking through stalls.

As for your trailer: I like the drawing distance/atmospheric feel the grass gives off when you lift the camera slightly. It makes the hand look very polished feel. :)

Thanks for sharing the dev log!

replies.author: Kiko_Production
replies.body:
Thanks! I’m glad you noticed the atmosphere when the camera lifts, that’s something I really wanted to get right.

And I agree, experimenting is a big part of the fun. My problem was knowing when an experiment had stopped teaching me anything and I was just repeating the same mistake with a slightly different prompt
